analysis.one_liner: Lets shooting victims sue gun makers and dealers by repealing the industry's lawsuit shield.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee on January 13, 2017, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2005 federal law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, generally blocks victims from suing gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and dealers when a firearm is criminally or unlawfully misused. This bill would repeal those protections, returning gun industry defendants to the same product-liability rules other businesses face. It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Shooting victims and their families, including people harmed by negligent sales or illegal distribution, would regain the ability to sue manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations in state or federal court.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2 through 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act (15 U.S.C. 7901-7903), which prohibit state and federal civil suits and administrative proceedings against firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations over criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm. [S2] [S3]

Restoring those suits would let victims use standard negligence and product-liability tools against dealers and manufacturers whose conduct enabled a shooting, a remedy currently barred by federal law. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, licensed dealers, importers, and gun industry trade associations, which would face civil lawsuits and potential damage awards they are currently shielded from; some litigation defense costs could ultimately be reflected in gun prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the current shield argue that a manufacturer or even a licensed dealer cannot reasonably control the criminal acts of a person who later misuses a legally sold firearm, and that repealing the shield would invite waves of lawsuits designed to punish the industry rather than compensate specific victims. [S2]

An honest supporter would acknowledge that opening the door to litigation also raises costs and legal risk for small, law-abiding gun dealers, and that courts could take years to sort which suits are legitimate. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is straightforward: it removes a special immunity no other major industry enjoys, giving shooting victims access to the courts they would have against any other negligent business. The strongest objection is not that gun makers should be liable for every criminal misuse of a legal product, but that sweeping litigation can be a backdoor effort to regulate firearms through damage awards rather than legislation; whether that is a bug or the point is precisely what a public debate over the bill never got to have.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee sent it to its Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittee on January 13, 2017, and it stayed there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress. [S1] [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Alcee Hastings introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress. [S1] [S2]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day of introduction. [S1] [S5]
On January 13, 2017, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, and the record shows no further action for the remainder of the Congress. [S1] [S5]
Only two members cosponsored the bill, both Democrats. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations kept the broad immunity from civil lawsuits over criminal misuse of firearms that the bill would have repealed, and shooting victims remained barred from bringing those suits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

for.name: 2 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only two cosponsors it received. [S4]

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Bob Goodlatte)
against.role: Committee of referral; controls whether bills get hearings or markups
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill saw no committee action for two years. [S1] [S5]

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats, and a bill repealing the gun industry's liability shield drew no Republican cosponsors in a Republican-controlled House; it received no committee or floor consideration. [S1] [S4]

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations
industries.note: The bill would have stripped the 2005 Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shield that bars most lawsuits over criminal misuse of firearms, exposing the industry to negligence and product-liability suits it currently cannot face. The industry's interest in the bill ran against shooting victims seeking to sue. [S2] [S3]
